title: Diabetic Foot Infection: Urgent Assessment, Imaging and Limb-Salvage Referral

evidenceAudit.scope: Adults with diabetes and a suspected foot infection in the emergency department (ED), diabetic foot clinic or ward: IWGDF/IDSA severity grade, osteomyelitis work-up, cultures, urgent surgical and vascular triggers, antibiotic pathway and durations. Uses the International Working Group on the Diabetic Foot / Infectious Diseases Society of America (IWGDF/IDSA) 2023 guideline and NICE NG19.
findings: Rebuilt from the thin 21 Oct 2026 version: IWGDF/IDSA classification, osteomyelitis tests with the ESR cut-off, surgical triggers, Pseudomonas and MRSA rules relevant to Saudi Arabia, six management steps and a duration comparison added.
IWGDF/IDSA and NICE NG19 differ on soft-tissue and osteomyelitis duration; both are shown side by side.
Doses trace to NICE NG19 Tables 1–2 opened on 22 Oct 2026.
unverifiedSections: No Saudi national diabetic foot infection guideline was found; IWGDF/IDSA Recommendation 15 (Asia or North Africa Pseudomonas rule) is applied for Saudi Arabia.
NICE NG19 does not rank the moderate/severe options; co-amoxiclav, the first listed, is marked preferred. Mild-infection alternatives are ordered as listed.

Gentamicin and metronidazole add-ons are named in NICE NG19 but not given as separate rows; doses: gentamicin initially 5–7 mg/kg once daily adjusted to levels, metronidazole 400 mg oral or 500 mg intravenous three times daily (NICE NG19, Table 2).
CKD and CLD lines come from the platform batch-01 table and were not re-opened in this task.
Statements on neuropathy and ulcer entry in Pathophysiology are clinical description, not taken from an opened section.
Typical adult reference ranges are not from the cited sources; local laboratory ranges apply.

pathophysiology.summary: Neuropathy and peripheral artery disease (PAD) allow unnoticed ulcers that become infected and spread to deep tissue and bone. Infection is graded by local signs, depth and systemic response (IWGDF/IDSA classification, AFP 2025 Table 1). Bone involvement (diabetes-related foot osteomyelitis) is common in moderate and severe infection and needs longer treatment (IWGDF/IDSA 2023, Recommendation 16). PAD limits antibiotic delivery and healing and needs urgent vascular assessment (IWGDF/IDSA 2023, Recommendation 20).
keyMechanisms: Neuropathic ulcer becomes the entry point.
Grade 2 mild: 2 or more local signs, erythema 0.5–2 cm (AFP 2025, Table 1).
Grade 3 moderate: erythema 2 cm or more or deeper tissue, no systemic signs; 3O with bone (AFP 2025, Table 1).
Grade 4 severe: 2 or more systemic signs (AFP 2025, Table 1).
PAD with ulcer or gangrene needs urgent vascular input (IWGDF/IDSA 2023, Recommendation 20).

symptoms: Pain or tenderness at the ulcer — may be absent with neuropathy (AFP 2025, Table 1).
Fever or rigors in severe infection (AFP 2025, Table 1).
physicalSigns: Swelling or induration, warmth and erythema around the wound (AFP 2025, Table 1).
Erythema 2 cm or more from the wound or infection deeper than subcutaneous tissue — moderate (AFP 2025, Table 1).
Positive probe-to-bone test suggests osteomyelitis (IWGDF/IDSA 2023, Recommendation 7).
Absent foot pulses or ischaemic changes — PAD (IWGDF/IDSA 2023, Recommendation 20).
redFlags: Two or more of: temperature above 38 °C or below 36 °C, heart rate above 90/min, respiratory rate above 20/min, white cells above 12 ×10⁹/L or over 10% bands — severe (AFP 2025, Table 1).
Extensive gangrene or necrotising infection (IWGDF/IDSA 2023, Recommendation 18).
Deep abscess or compartment syndrome (IWGDF/IDSA 2023, Recommendation 18).
precipitants: Recent hospital stay, antibiotics, haemodialysis or nursing home — methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) risk (IWGDF/IDSA 2023, Table 4).
Macerated ulcer or warm climate — Pseudomonas risk (IWGDF/IDSA 2023, Table 4).

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Warm, swollen foot without a wound or with intact skin; bone changes on imaging.
Acute joint inflammation without an ulcer; crystals on aspiration.
No local or systemic signs (grade 1); do not give antibiotics (IWGDF/IDSA 2023, Recommendation 11).
Calf swelling without a foot portal of entry.

diagnosticCriteria.threshold: Grade 1 uninfected; 2 mild; 3 moderate (3O with bone); 4 severe (4O with bone) (AFP 2025, Table 1).

Probe-to-bone, plain X-ray and erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR), C-reactive protein (CRP) or procalcitonin together; ESR 70 mm/h or more supports osteomyelitis (sensitivity 81%, specificity 80%) (IWGDF/IDSA 2023, Recommendation 7).
magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) (IWGDF/IDSA 2023, Recommendation 8); bone biopsy when the diagnosis or organism is uncertain (AFP 2025).

clinicalManagement.title: Grade infection and perfusion
actions: Assign IWGDF/IDSA grade (see Diagnostic criteria) (AFP 2025, Table 1).
Do not give antibiotics for an uninfected ulcer (IWGDF/IDSA 2023, Recommendation 11).

clinicalManagement.title: Cultures before antibiotics
clinicalManagement.timeframe: Before the first dose when safe
actions: Take aseptic tissue by curettage or biopsy, not a swab (IWGDF/IDSA 2023, Recommendation 5).

clinicalManagement.title: Call surgery urgently
clinicalManagement.timeframe: Same day; consider surgery within 24–48 hours
actions: Urgent surgical consultation for severe infection, or moderate infection with extensive gangrene, necrotising infection, deep abscess, compartment syndrome or severe ischaemia (IWGDF/IDSA 2023, Recommendation 18).
Consider early surgery within 24–48 hours with antibiotics for moderate and severe infection (IWGDF/IDSA 2023, Recommendation 19).
PAD with ulcer or gangrene: urgent vascular consultation (IWGDF/IDSA 2023, Recommendation 20).

clinicalManagement.title: Start the antibiotic branch
clinicalManagement.timeframe: Within the first hour if severe
actions: Mild: oral branch (see Medicines) (NICE NG19, Table 1).
Moderate or severe: backbone antibiotic; severe intravenous for at least 48 hours until stable (NICE NG19, Table 2).
Add anti-MRSA or antipseudomonal cover only with the risk factors in Medicines (IWGDF/IDSA 2023, Recommendations 14–15).

clinicalManagement.title: Set duration
actions: Soft tissue: 1–2 weeks; up to 3–4 weeks if extensive, slow or severe PAD (IWGDF/IDSA 2023, Recommendation 12).
Osteomyelitis without resection: up to 6 weeks; after minor amputation with a positive bone margin: up to 3 weeks (IWGDF/IDSA 2023, Recommendation 16).
Review intravenous treatment by 48 hours and switch to oral (NICE NG19, Table 2).

clinicalManagement.title: Off-load and follow up
actions: Off-load pressure and continue wound care in the diabetic foot service.
Follow osteomyelitis for at least 6 months after antibiotics end to confirm remission (IWGDF/IDSA 2023, Recommendation 17).

branches.label: Mild infection
branches.entryCriteria: IWGDF/IDSA grade 2: skin and subcutaneous tissue only, erythema 0.5–2 cm, no systemic signs

branches.label: Pseudomonas suspected or confirmed
branches.entryCriteria: Moderate or severe infection with Pseudomonas isolated from the site in recent weeks, or macerated ulcer in a warm climate; replaces the backbone

branches.label: MRSA suspected or confirmed — add-on
branches.entryCriteria: Previous MRSA infection or colonisation, or recent admission, recent antibiotics, haemodialysis or nursing-home residence; added to the backbone

medicationPlan.note: Choose one branch for the backbone; one antibiotic per step. Add one anti-MRSA agent only when risk factors are present. Do not treat a clinically uninfected ulcer. Paediatric, penicillin-allergy, chronic kidney disease (CKD) and chronic liver disease (CLD) lines on every row; CKD and CLD lines need pharmacist confirmation. SFDA registration not verified.

learningObjectives: Grade diabetic foot infection with IWGDF/IDSA criteria.
Know when surgery and vascular review are urgent.
keyPoints: ESR 70 mm/h or more supports osteomyelitis.
pitfalls: Missing ischaemia in a neuropathic foot.
Routine anti-Pseudomonas cover without risk factors.
Stopping follow-up before 6 months in osteomyelitis.
